en.title: One Mediator Does Not Exclude the Saints
en.question: 1 Timothy 2:5 says there is "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Doesn't this text directly forbid asking saints to intercede?

answer.summary:
> "The fact that other mediators exist between God and man does not exclude the one mediator." — St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, III, Q. 26, A. 1

1 Timothy 2:5 is the most-cited Protestant objection to the intercession of saints: "For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." The objection assumes that "one mediator" means "only intercessor" — that no other person can bring a prayer or request before God. But this reading collapses immediately when applied to the broader context of the same passage, and it conflicts with Paul's own consistent practice elsewhere.

The very passage that declares "one mediator" opens with Paul's exhortation: "I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people" (1 Timothy 2:1). Paul is asking living Christians to intercede for one another — and he himself regularly requests such intercession (Romans 15:30, 2 Corinthians 1:11, Ephesians 6:19, Colossians 4:3). If the "one mediator" text forbade any intercessory role for anyone other than Christ, it would eliminate all Christian intercessory prayer — not just prayer to the saints. The Protestant who prays "Lord, please help my friend" is also acting as a mediator in the broad sense. The text cannot mean what the objection claims, because the text itself immediately commands the practice it supposedly forbids.

The resolution lies in distinguishing the unique mediation of Christ from the participatory, dependent intercession of others. Christ is the one Mediator in the absolute sense: he alone reconciles humanity to God by his incarnation, sacrifice, and resurrection. He alone atones; he alone merits grace; he alone opens heaven. All other "mediation" is derived from his and dependent on it — not a rival mediation but a participation in Christ's. When a Christian asks another Christian (living or dead) to pray for them, they are not bypassing Christ; they are involving another member of Christ's Body in an act of intercession that reaches God only through Christ. St. Thomas Aquinas drew this distinction precisely: secondary mediators do not compete with the one Mediator but serve as channels of his grace.

The difference between asking a living Christian and a canonized saint is not one of principle but of certainty of effectiveness. When a Catholic asks St. Thomas Aquinas to pray for them, they are confident that Thomas is alive in Christ (Matthew 22:32, "he is not God of the dead, but of the living"), that he is present before God (Revelation 7:9–10), and that his prayers are offered with perfect charity undistorted by earthly weakness or sin. James 5:16 affirms that "the prayer of a righteous man has great power in its effects" — and the saints in glory are supremely righteous, their righteousness no longer obscured.

The Catechism (CCC 956) states: "Being more closely united to Christ, those who dwell in heaven fix the whole Church more firmly in holiness... They do not cease to intercede with the Father for us, as they proffer the merits which they acquired on earth through the one mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus." The mediation of Christ is not diminished by the intercession of saints — it is glorified in it, as his Body acts in his name before his Father.
